title: Numbers & Math
summary: Numbers let JavaScript measure, count, and calculate.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: Use `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/` for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Parentheses make the order clear. It is like writing a calculation on paper. JavaScript may convert values during `+`, so convert inputs deliberately when they come from text fields. For example, a form value `"12"` needs conversion before arithmetic; otherwise `+` may join text.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: `Number("12")` converts numeric text into the number 12. Invalid numeric text becomes `NaN`. It is like reading a string on a label and checking whether it represents a usable quantity. Validate input before using it, and do not assume an empty field means zero. For example, check an input with `Number.isFinite` before using it in a total.

subtopics.title: Common choice
subtopics.explanation: `NaN` means a numeric operation did not produce a usable number. It is unusual because it is not equal to itself, so use `Number.isNaN(value)` to check it. It is like a calculator display showing an invalid result. Handle this state with a clear validation message. For example, use `Number.isNaN` to recognize an invalid conversion, not equality with NaN.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: Rounding changes the displayed or stored value. For prices, repeated floating-point calculations can create tiny precision errors. It is like splitting a cent into pieces that cash registers cannot represent exactly. Choose a consistent monetary representation, such as integer minor units, and round at a deliberate boundary. For example, for money, store cents as whole numbers or use a decimal library with explicit rounding.

subtopics.title: Use it safely
subtopics.explanation: Check user input before using it in a calculation. Confirm it is present, numeric, and within the allowed range. It is like checking a measurement before cutting material. Clear validation prevents confusing outputs and helps protect later code from assumptions that are not true. For example, reject negative quantities when the business rule allows only zero or more.

foundations.overview: JavaScript uses the `number` type for ordinary whole numbers and decimals. Operators perform arithmetic, while conversion and rounding need care. Think of a calculator that stores one common kind of numeric value. Check user input before calculating, and use explicit rules for money because binary floating-point values can produce surprising decimal results.
foundations.whyItMatters: Numeric mistakes can affect totals, limits, and user trust. Convert values deliberately, check invalid results, and make precision rules visible to anyone reviewing the code.
foundations.browserPerspective: Engines like V8 optimize integers that fit in a small range ('Smi') for speed and fall back to full doubles for larger or fractional values. This is invisible to you, but it is why integer-heavy code can be faster than float-heavy code.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Calculating cart totals (often in integer cents to avoid float errors), rounding prices with toFixed, generating random ids or dice rolls with Math.random, parsing user-typed numbers from inputs, and handling large database ids with BigInt.
foundations.businessImpact: Money math done in floats can produce off-by-a-cent totals that erode trust and fail audits; handling precision correctly protects revenue accuracy and compliance.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing the safe-integer limit, the right parser, and how to compare floats prevents a whole category of silent bugs in calculations and conditionals.
foundations.performanceImpact: Integer operations within the safe range are fast and exact; BigInt is slower than regular numbers, so reserve it for cases that genuinely exceed the safe-integer limit.

commonMisconceptions.myth: 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is true, and if not it's a JavaScript bug.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's false because IEEE 754 binary floats cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly; this happens in nearly every language, so compare within a tolerance or use integer cents.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can check for NaN with x === NaN.
commonMisconceptions.reality: NaN is never equal to itself, so x === NaN is always false; use Number.isNaN(x) instead.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Rounding only changes how a number looks.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Rounding can change stored data too, so decide whether it belongs in calculation or display.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Any text can be safely converted to zero.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Invalid or empty input needs an explicit validation decision instead of a silent default.

visualExplorer.caption: Trace how binary floating point introduces a tiny rounding error.

config.intro: Follow the addition 0.1 + 0.2 as the engine stores and adds these values in binary.

steps.name: Store 0.1
steps.detail: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so it is stored as the nearest 64-bit float (slightly above 0.1).

steps.name: Store 0.2
steps.detail: 0.2 also cannot be represented exactly and is stored as the nearest float (slightly above 0.2).

steps.name: Add the approximations
steps.detail: The two slightly-off values are added, and the small errors combine.

steps.name: Round the result
steps.detail: The sum is rounded to the nearest representable double, which is 0.30000000000000004.

steps.name: Compare to 0.3
steps.detail: 0.3 stored as a float differs from that sum, so 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is false.

steps.name: Compare safely
steps.detail: Check Math.abs(sum - 0.3) < 1e-9 (a tolerance) instead of strict equality.

interactiveExamples.title: Floating-point in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: See the classic precision result and how to compare floats safely with a small tolerance (epsilon).

sandbox.code:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);            // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);    // false

const nearlyEqual = Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 1e-9;
console.log('close enough?', nearlyEqual); // true

codeLab.title: Sum prices without float errors
codeLab.instructions: Write total(prices) that sums an array of dollar amounts and returns the result rounded to 2 decimals as a number. Avoid floating-point drift by working in integer cents internally.
hints: Multiply each price by 100 and round to get exact integer cents.
Sum the cents, divide by 100, then toFixed(2) and wrap in Number().
